messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 65

The first message arrives on a Tuesday in his final semester at the university design program. It is polite at first, requesting feedback on a layout, but the replies stop arriving after a week. He does not notice the shift in his apartment door handle until he comes home from the library to find a single origami crane resting on his welcome mat. By November, the digital boundary dissolves. His inbox fills with screenshots of his private sketchbook pages, time-stamped from three weeks prior. He changes his passwords, deletes his social accounts, and rents a different room on the third floor of a walk-up building. He tells no one. The silence in his head becomes a constant hum. He learns to measure safety in seconds. The time it takes to lock the deadbolt. The number of camera blind spots along his commute. He stops attending evening critiques. His friends’ invitations disappear into a graveyard of unread notifications. When he closes his eyes, he does not dream; he replays the sound of his own door handle turning, the exact pitch of his own breathing, the way his pulse catches when he sees the same gray jacket in a crowded coffee shop. He stops drinking coffee. He avoids mirrors. He tells himself he is just tired, but his body has already drafted its own emergency manual. Every sudden sound fractures his focus. Every unfamiliar phone number stops his hands. He calls his mother in Lagos once a week, but the conversations grow shorter. He leaves on "good" first, a practiced exit before the silence stretches too thin, his voice tightening around the edges of a language that suddenly feels too close to home. He takes a remote contract as a UX designer, hoping the familiar architecture of user flows will ground him. He approaches mapping intuitive journeys as a way to predict where a user’s finger travels, smoothing the friction from a digital experience. Now, he designs digital barricades. He spends his days stress-testing his own interfaces for loopholes, building redundant confirmations, darkening default themes. His cursor hovers over every button twice. He watches his own analytics with the same scrutiny he once reserved for security cameras, tracking where users hesitate, where they drop off, as if debugging a system that might betray him. He maps his apartment like a wireframe, identifying every angle where someone could watch him. The work pays the rent, but it drains him. He works in ninety-minute bursts, then stares at a blank canvas until the panic subsides. He tells himself he is being thorough. He knows it is not the same. Now, at nineteen, he sits in my office with his knees pressed together and his hands folded over his knees. His gaze tracks the door the moment we begin speaking. He answers in careful, measured sentences, but his right foot taps a rapid, syncopated rhythm against the floorboard. When I ask about his weekend, he lists his actions like inventory checks: locks the door, checks the hallway camera, walks the perimeter of the block. He pauses, swallows, and looks at his shoes. The air conditioning kicks on, and he flinches before he even registers the sound. He exhales slowly, as if releasing tension he has been holding since the beginning of the conversation. His shoulders drop a fraction, then rise again when the clock on the wall ticks. He watches my hands rest on the desk, measuring their distance from the door, from him, from the window. His breathing has already synchronized with the rhythm of his own footsteps, counting steps, counting heartbeats, counting the moments until he can leave. He does not look away from the exit.
